photo.description: United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon addresses the crowd after Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord as U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry sat in a plaza outside the Cartagena Indias Convention Center in Cartagena, Colombia, on September 26, 2016, while attending a peace ceremony between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that ended a five-decade conflict. pages.text: Colombia had a very long war. The government and the FARC rebel group wanted to stop fighting. They started peace talks in the city of Havana, Cuba in the year 2012 to find a good way to end the conflict.

In 2016, the leaders signed a final peace agreement. President Juan Manuel Santos and rebel commander Rodrigo Londoño made peace. But the people voted on the agreement in October 2016. Sadly, more voters said no than yes to the plan.
The leaders did not give up. They made a new and changed agreement. On November 24, 2016, they signed this new plan. They sent it to Congress instead of holding another vote for the public to decide.
Both houses of the Colombian Congress looked at the new agreement. They voted to approve it at the end of November 2016. This official vote finally brought the long armed conflict to an end.
Many other countries and groups helped with the peace process. The United Nations also helped to watch and support the peace. Women joined the talks too, asking to be a big part of building peace.

B1-B2.headline: Ending Decades of Conflict in Colombia

pages.text: The Colombian peace process refers to formal negotiations between the government under President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC-EP guerrilla group. Their goal was to end a decades-long conflict. These historic talks began in September 2012 and were held mostly in Havana, Cuba.

In 2016, leaders announced a final agreement. President Santos and FARC commander Rodrigo Londoño signed the first accord. However, when the agreement was put to a national referendum on October 2, 2016, it was narrowly rejected by voters, with 50.2% voting against the deal.

Following the surprising defeat at the ballot box, negotiators quickly drafted a revised peace agreement. This new version was signed on November 24, 2016. Instead of organizing another public referendum, the government submitted the text directly to the Congress of Colombia for ratification.

Both houses of Congress reviewed and approved the new agreement on November 29 and 30, 2016. This legislative approval officially brought the long-running conflict to an end. The process had also involved secret exploratory meetings that started back in the spring of 2011.

Throughout the negotiations, the international community played a major role as a facilitator and guarantor. The United Nations Security Council even adopted unanimous resolutions to support the peace talks and help monitor compliance, ensuring strong global backing for the Colombian peace efforts.

C1-C2.headline: The Architecture of the Colombian Peace Accord

pages.text: The Colombian peace process encompasses the protracted negotiations executed between the administration of President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC-EP insurgency. Commencing formally in September 2012 primarily within Havana, Cuba, these diplomatic efforts sought to terminate an internal armed conflict that originated decades prior in 1964.

Subsequent to years of dialogue, leadership announced a final accord in 2016, signed by President Santos and insurgent commander Rodrigo Londoño Echeverri. Nevertheless, this initial iteration suffered a narrow defeat during the national plebiscite on October 2, 2016, wherein 50.2% of participating voters rejected the proposed terms.

Demonstrating institutional resilience, the negotiating parties formulated a revised peace agreement, which was duly signed on November 24, 2016. Eschewing a secondary public referendum, the executive branch elected to submit the revised text to the bicameral Congress of Colombia for legislative ratification.

Both legislative chambers ratified the instrument on November 29 and 30, 2016, thereby concluding the historical hostilities. This political resolution followed a complex trajectory that included clandestine preliminary meetings in 2011, transitional justice frameworks, and targeted mine clearance initiatives.

Notably, the peace architecture distinguished itself through extensive international mediation and institutional guarantees. The United Nations Security Council lent unprecedented unanimous backing via resolutions like S/RES/2261, establishing an external verification mechanism to monitor compliance with the finalized terms.
